narrative.text: Front matter of the Digital transformation handbook for reporting substandard and falsified medical products (ISBN 978-92-4-012074-7 electronic, 978-92-4-012075-4 print; © WHO 2026, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO), including suggested citation, CIP data, licensing terms, general disclaimers, and the table of contents.

Acknowledges the handbook's authors (Swaroop Jayaprakash, Natschja Nash-Mendez, Rutendo Kuwana, Leticia Megias, Christian Moretti Anfossi), technical reviewers and contributors (WHO headquarters, United Health Futures, independent experts), national regulatory authorities in Chile (ISP) and South Africa (SAHPRA), and funding from the Gates Foundation and the UK Fleming Fund.
Structured table of 19 abbreviations and acronyms used across the handbook, including BPMN, DIIG, FHIR, GSMS, HL7, ICT, ID, ITU, LMICs, M&E, NMRA, PMS, RACI, Rb-PMS, SaaS, SMART, UAT, UHF, and WHO.

Structured glossary defining 35 key terms used in the handbook, including active and passive pharmacovigilance, adverse drug reactions, business process, data element, digitization, digitalization, digital transformation, enabling environment, enterprise architecture, falsified and substandard medical products, functional and non-functional requirements, interoperability, Member State Mechanism (MSM), polypharmacy, post-market surveillance (PMS), registry, SMART Guidelines, trade item, unregistered product, user acceptance testing (UAT), and workflow.

Introduces the public health, antimicrobial resistance, and socioeconomic threats posed by substandard and falsified medical products, states the agreed WHO/Member State definitions, explains how supply chain complexity and procurement pressures increase risk in LMICs, and highlights the role of risk-based post-market surveillance (Rb-PMS) and NMRAs.

Explains how reporting suspected substandard and falsified medical products enables NMRA investigation, market removal, and global surveillance via the WHO Global Surveillance and Monitoring System (GSMS), notes the frontline role and under-reporting of health care professionals, and motivates transitioning from paper-based reporting to standards-based digital solutions such as smartphone applications piloted in Indonesia and the United Republic of Tanzania.

Defines the target audience for the handbook and presents Table 1 mapping each of the seven handbook chapters/phases to illustrative target organizations, target user teams and roles, and section purpose.

Outlines four implementation scenarios for using the handbook, prerequisites around national digital health and supply chain strategies, alignment with the WHO Digital implementation investment guide (DIIG) across seven enterprise phases (Fig. 1), and alignment with WHO SMART Guidelines knowledge layers L1–L5 (Fig. 2).

Describes the development of the handbook through global consultations with health care professionals, NMRAs, and Member States, pilot implementations in Indonesia and the United Republic of Tanzania, and alignment with the Principles for Digital Development, DIIG, and the WHO/ITU National eHealth strategy toolkit.

Chapter 1 opener outlining the inputs, outputs (situational analysis report and stakeholder matrix), and reference resources required to assess the current state and enabling environment before implementing a digital reporting system.

Guides stakeholder identification and analysis across government, health care providers, funders, industry, implementers, and civil society, and presents Table 2 with sample stakeholder analysis questions across six dimensions (roles and responsibilities, information flows, influence and power, interests and expectations, engagement and collaboration, and capacity and resources).

Outlines the six areas of a country digital readiness assessment (national digital health strategy, enabling policy and regulatory environment, governance framework, human resources, technology infrastructure, and security and privacy protection) and presents Table 3 on assessing network coverage, hardware/software availability, infrastructure, security, privacy, and data ownership.

Provides guidance on evaluating current substandard and falsified reporting practices, data collection forms, digital tools, and reporting barriers, presenting Table 4 (assessing pharmacovigilance and SF reporting practices and data usage), Table 5 (common challenges and barriers across seven categories with potential solutions, including anonymous reporting considerations), and the Chapter 1 checklist.

Chapter 2 opener summarizing the inputs, outputs (new/amended regulatory policies, governance structures, and strategic goals), and resources for establishing a shared understanding and governance framework.

Guides the review of national regulatory frameworks supporting digital reporting of substandard and falsified medical products, covering pharmacovigilance and quality surveillance integration, mandatory and voluntary reporting obligations, and enforcement mechanisms.
Describes multisectoral policy alignment across law enforcement and customs, health financing and procurement agencies, innovation and ICT ministries, and regional and global regulatory authorities.

Defines a three-tier governance structure (national steering committee, technical working group, and advisory council) and key leadership roles (ministry of health/NMRA, project champion, and digital health coordinator/project manager).
Explains how to set SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) strategic goals for the substandard and falsified medical product reporting application.

Categorizes technical, financial, and political/stakeholder risks in digital transformation, references the risk management template in Annex 7, and concludes Chapter 2 with the end-of-chapter checklist.

Chapter 3 opener detailing the inputs, outputs (digital investment roadmap and new or revised digital health enterprise architecture), and resources for defining the future state of the reporting solution.

Guides the development of a phased digital investment roadmap across short-term (1–2 years), medium-term (3–5 years), and long-term (5+ years) horizons, accompanied by Table 6 mapping 22 system attributes across five categories to short-, medium-, and long-term priorities.

Explains how to situate the substandard and falsified reporting application as a point-of-service application within the DIIG digital health enterprise architecture framework (Fig. 3), emphasizing open standards and interoperability (TOGAF, HL7 FHIR), cybersecurity and data protection, and the Chapter 3 checklist.

Chapter 4 opener listing the inputs, documentation outputs (user personas, user scenarios, as-is and to-be business processes, data dictionary, decision logic algorithms, functional and non-functional requirements, and indicators), and resources for determining system requirements.

Defines user personas for skilled health care professionals and related individuals, presenting Table 7 (examples of key user personas: Doctor, Nurse, Community health worker, Laboratory technician, and Pharmacist with descriptions, alternative titles, and ISCO codes) and Table 8 (related user persona: Individual).

Explains how user scenarios translate personas into practical use cases and presents Table 9 detailing typical end-to-end reporting scenarios (discovery, initial action, accessing reporting app, completing the report, submitting the report, and follow-up/feedback) across nine health care professions.

Describes how to inventory business processes and map as-is and to-be workflows using BPMN 2.0 conventions, presenting Table 10 (business process matrix example SF-REP-001 for suspect product detection and reporting by a pharmacist) and Fig. 4 (example BPMN workflow for reporting substandard and falsified medical products).

Explains the role of a standards-based data dictionary (ICD-11, SNOMED-GPS, HL7 FHIR) and presents Table 11 defining 10 illustrative data elements (SFR.A1.DE1 to SFR.A1.DE10) for activity SFR.A1 (Report substandard or falsified product).

Presents illustrative functional and non-functional requirements for the reporting application in Table 12 (7 user-story functional requirements under SFR.FXNREQ.001–002) and Table 13 (97 non-functional requirements across security, system requirements, scalability, usability, configuration, interoperability, hardware/connectivity, and delivery), followed by the Chapter 4 checklist.

Chapter 5 covering implementation planning and budgeting, including the chapter opener (inputs, outputs, resources), Table 14 (steps across implementation planning, budget development, and execution), evaluation of deployment and software options, Table 15 (advantages, considerations, and challenges of five software options), and the Chapter 5 checklist.
Chapter 6 opener outlining the inputs, outputs (M&E plan and operations and sustainability plan), and reference resources for monitoring, evaluating, and scaling the reporting application.

Distinguishes intrinsic monitoring from extrinsic evaluation across the digital health maturity life cycle (Fig. 5 and Fig. 6), and provides Table 16 (sample evaluation questions across usability, efficacy, effectiveness, and cost), Table 17 (six steps in developing a comprehensive M&E plan), and Table 18 (reference measures across quality, fidelity, stability, functionality, and investment).

Guides the development of an operations, continuous improvement, and sustainability plan covering stakeholder ownership, infrastructure and maintenance resources, recurring knowledge management and training, financial planning, backups and redundancy, and change management, concluding with the Chapter 6 checklist.

Chapter 7 presenting the WHO-coordinated pilot case study in Indonesia and the United Republic of Tanzania (36 reports of 27 medical products), including the 4-step reporting workflow, offline and multilingual app functions, and a structured evaluation table of successes and areas requiring improvement across application/reporting and feasibility.
Lists the 37 numbered bibliographic references cited throughout the handbook, with footnote 1 noting that all references were accessed on 23 April 2026.

Lists 17 key WHO, ITU, UNICEF, MEASURE Evaluation, HL7 FHIR, and Open Group reference resources and toolkits supporting digital health transformation and substandard and falsified medical product reporting.
Part divider introducing Annexes 1–7 of the handbook.

Annex 1 presenting the nine Principles for Digital Development (Understand the existing ecosystem; Share, reuse and improve; Design with people; Design for inclusion; Build for sustainability; Establish people-first data practices; Create open and transparent practices; Anticipate and mitigate harms; Use evidence to improve outcomes) and their definitions.

Annex 2 providing a structured user persona template and worksheet covering persona occupation, demographics, expected daily/weekly/monthly roles and responsibilities, behaviour patterns, context description, challenges/pain points, and definition of success.

Annex 3 defining 15 key Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN 2.0) symbols (Pool, Swim lane, Start event, Start event message, End event, Activity/task, Activity with subprocess, Activity with a business rule, Sequence flow, Message flow, Exclusive gateway, Parallel gateway, Throw – link event, Catch – link event, Ad hoc subprocess, and Loop activity).

Annex 4 providing a sample stakeholder RACI (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) matrix template mapping project activities (Define project scope, Gather requirements, Design UI/UX) across NMRA, Ministry of health, Implementation partner, Medical product industry, Health care professionals, and other stakeholders.

Annex 5 providing a matrix template for assessing the current software applications landscape across 12 supply chain and regulatory domains and 7 health system actors, illustrating deployed systems (Planning system, OpenLMIS, ERP, RapidSMS, OpenClinic, NPC, Registration system) and in-progress tools (Health analytics platform, Pharmacovigilance mobile app, NPC mobile app).

Annex 6 presenting an example barrier analysis mapping 15 barriers across 7 barrier categories (Health care, NMRA-related, Technology, Economic, Social, Education and knowledge, and Capacity barriers) to the affected stakeholders (Health care professionals, NMRA, and Consumer).

Annex 7 providing a risk management template illustrated with sample risk 001 (Inadequate training: IF/THEN description, priority Low, impact Major, probability Medium, status Mitigate, three mitigation steps, and raised/reviewed dates).
